questions.text: A contractor installs structural fill and claims it is '100% Proctor compacted.' The project engineer should be skeptical of this claim. Explain why.

options.text: 100% Proctor is not possible; the Proctor test determines the maximum achievable density, and field compaction cannot exceed this laboratory maximum (under standard conditions).
100% Proctor is easily achieved with modern equipment; the claim is credible and requires no further verification.
100% Proctor means the fill is perfect and requires no further testing or quality assurance monitoring.
100% Proctor is impossible because the contractor has different equipment than the lab and cannot replicate conditions.

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: The Standard Proctor test defines γd_max in a controlled laboratory environment with specific energy input (manual compaction). Field compaction uses different equipment and conditions (rollers, variable compaction energy) and cannot, in practice, exceed the lab maximum under standard conditions. Achieving 100% Proctor in the field is theoretically possible but practically very rare. A claim of 100% Proctor should be met with skepticism; the contractor may not understand the test or may be inflating the claim. Typical field compaction is 90–95% Proctor. Verification via field density test is essential.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: ASTM D698 (Standard Proctor Test); NSCP 2015 (Fill Compaction Requirements)

questions.text: A building on soft clay exhibits 80 mm differential settlement between corner and center columns over 3 years. Cracking appears in partition walls. The soil consolidation coefficient is cv = 0.5 m²/year. Analyze whether consolidation is complete and what design action is appropriate.

options.text: Consolidation is definitely complete at 3 years; the building will not settle further. Cracking is a construction defect, not a foundation issue, and requires immediate repair

Consolidation may still be ongoing. With cv = 0.5 m²/year and clay depth H = 8 m (typical), time to 90% consolidation is T90 ≈ (H²/cv) × 0.848 ≈ (64/0.5) × 0.848 ≈ 108 years. After 3 years, consolidation is only a small fraction complete. Future settlement will continue over decades, causing additional cracking. Design action: monitor settlement, install crack gauges, underpinning provisions, and differential settlement tolerances.
Soft clay never consolidates; settlement is permanent and cannot be calculated, making any design action futile
80 mm differential settlement is normal and acceptable for any building type, requiring no further action or monitoring

rationale.a: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: Consolidation rate is governed by cv and soil layer thickness. For soft clay (cv often 0.1–1 m²/year) and deep deposits, consolidation to 90% completion can take 100–200+ years. At 3 years, only a small fraction of primary consolidation may be complete. Future settlement is inevitable and will cause additional cracking. Design must anticipate this: monitor settlement, establish tolerance limits (50–80 mm differential for office buildings), install crack gauges, provide underpinning provisions in critical areas, and warn the client of continued movement. This is not a failure; it is a design reality for buildings on soft clay.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: Bowles (1996); Terzaghi et al. (1996); NSCP 2015 (Settlement Monitoring)

questions.text: Distinguish between immediate (elastic) settlement and primary consolidation settlement in terms of mechanism, soil type, and duration.

options.text: Immediate and primary are the same process; naming is arbitrary, and there is no significant difference in their effects

Immediate settlement is elastic compression of soil solids and air expulsion without pore water drainage (fast, hours to days). Primary consolidation is pore water expulsion from clay under constant load (slow, months to years). Immediate: all soil types; significant in sand. Primary: clay and silt dominant; minor in sand. Sand settles fast (immediate); clay settles slow (primary consolidation).
Immediate settlement occurs in clay; primary consolidation occurs in sand, which is contrary to typical soil behavior
Primary consolidation is faster than immediate settlement, which contradicts the usual understanding of soil mechanics

rationale.a: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: Immediate settlement is elastic deformation and rapid air expulsion, occurring in hours to days in all soils. Primary consolidation is pore water expulsion and volume reduction in clay under constant load, occurring in months to years. Sand has high permeability; pore water drains quickly and primary settlement is minor. Clay has low permeability; pore water drains slowly and primary settlement is dominant. This is the fundamental distinction between soil types and settlement behavior.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: NSCP 2015, Chapter 1-C; Bowles (1996); Terzaghi et al. (1996)

questions.text: A soft clay layer (H = 10 m, c = 30 kPa, φ = 15°) underlies a building. Explain how bearing capacity is affected by (a) increasing footing depth Df, (b) increasing footing width B, and (c) lowering the groundwater level.

options.text: Bearing capacity is unaffected by Df, B, or groundwater; it depends only on cohesion and friction angle, which are intrinsic soil properties unaffected by external changes

Df increases bearing capacity (larger depth factor). B has minimal effect on ultimate bearing capacity per unit area qu (independent of B for sands; slight increase for clays per shape factors). Total capacity qult × B × L increases with B. Lowering groundwater increases effective stress in the saturated zone, increasing bearing capacity.

Df decreases bearing capacity (deeper = higher surcharge, lower bearing capacity). B decreases bearing capacity (wider footings settle more). Groundwater has no effect on bearing capacity, as it does not alter the soil's inherent properties
All three factors decrease bearing capacity, leading to potential structural instability and increased risk of settlement

rationale.a: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: Bearing capacity is affected by multiple factors beyond cohesion and friction angle. (a) Depth factor increases bearing capacity as Df increases; deeper footings have higher bearing capacity due to confining pressure. (b) Width factor is complex: larger B can support larger total load, but bearing capacity per unit area depends on stress distribution. Very large B (mat foundations) flatten pressure but load-carrying capacity is still substantial. (c) Lowering groundwater increases effective stress in the zone above the water table, increasing bearing capacity in that zone. These are standard factors in bearing capacity equations (Terzaghi, Meyerhof, Hansen).
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A building foundation settles 10 mm in the first week after construction and another 5 mm over the next 6 months. The soil is soft clay with low permeability. Identify the settlement types occurring and explain the time-dependent behavior.

options.text: Only immediate settlement occurs; the 10 mm in week 1 is all the settlement the building will ever experience, which is unlikely given the soil type

Week 1 (10 mm) is immediate (elastic) settlement. Months 1–6 (5 mm additional) is primary consolidation as pore water slowly drains from the clay under the footing pressure. In soft clay, primary consolidation continues over months to years; the 5 mm over 6 months will likely continue, perhaps with decreasing rate, for 2–3 more years.
All 15 mm is primary consolidation; no immediate settlement occurs in clay, which contradicts typical settlement behavior
The building is failing; all 15 mm indicates a structural problem, which is an overstatement without further evidence

rationale.a: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: In soft clay, immediate settlement occurs rapidly (within hours to days) as soils solids compress elastically. Primary consolidation follows over months to years as pore water drains and soil volume reduces under constant load. The 10 mm in week 1 is immediate settlement. The 5 mm over 6 months is the beginning of primary consolidation. In soft clay, the total primary settlement can exceed 50–100 mm and take 2–5 years to complete. This is normal; the building must be designed for this movement (differential settlement limits, monitoring).
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A Standard Proctor compaction test produces γd_max = 18.5 kN/m³ at OMC = 11%. A field density test on the building pad shows γd_field = 16.8 kN/m³ at w = 10.5%. Determine if the field fill complies with a '90% Proctor at OMC ± 2%' specification.

options.text: Yes, it complies. Field moisture 10.5% is within OMC ± 2% (9–13%); field density 16.8 kN/m³ ÷ 18.5 kN/m³ = 90.8%, which exceeds 90%. Specification is satisfied.
No, it does not comply. Field moisture 10.5% is outside the OMC ± 2% range, which is critical for achieving the required compaction.
Yes, it always complies because the field density is above 16 kN/m³, which is generally considered adequate for most construction purposes.
No, it does not comply because the field density is not equal to the lab maximum, which is necessary for full compliance with the specification.

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: Compliance requires two conditions: (1) field moisture within OMC ± 2%, and (2) field density ≥ 90% γd_max. Field moisture 10.5% is within 11% ± 2% (range 9–13%), satisfying condition 1. Field density 16.8 / 18.5 = 90.8% ≥ 90%, satisfying condition 2. Both conditions are met; the fill complies. However, note: 90.8% is barely above the 90% threshold, leaving no margin for additional testing or variation. Future density tests should verify continued compliance.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: ASTM D698 (Standard Proctor Test); ASTM D2922 (Field Density Test)

questions.text: What is the primary purpose of compaction in structural fill, and what does the specification '90% Proctor at OMC ± 2%' mean?

options.text: Compaction removes all air voids; 90% Proctor means 90% of all voids are eliminated, which is a common misconception

Compaction increases soil density and bearing capacity, and reduces future settlement. The specification means the field fill must achieve 90% of the dry unit weight determined by the Standard Proctor lab test, at the lab-determined optimum moisture content ± 2%.
Compaction is aesthetic; the percentage is arbitrary, often misunderstood in engineering contexts
90% Proctor means 90% of the fill is water; the rest is air, which is incorrect but sometimes believed

rationale.a: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: Compaction densifies soil to increase bearing capacity and reduce compressibility. The Standard Proctor test identifies γd max (maximum dry unit weight) at OMC (optimum moisture content, typically 10–15%). A specification of 90% Proctor means field compaction must achieve γd_field ≥ 0.90 × γd_max at moisture within OMC ± 2%. This is a quantitative, verifiable requirement.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: NSCP 2015, Chapter 1-C; ASTM D698 (Standard Proctor Test)

questions.text: Explain the relationship between soil grain size classification (clay, silt, sand, gravel) and bearing capacity, compressibility, and drainage characteristics.

options.text: Grain size does not affect bearing capacity, compressibility, or drainage; all soils behave identically, which is a common misconception

Clay (fine-grained, < 0.005 mm) has high compressibility, poor drainage, and moderate bearing capacity (depends on cohesion and consolidation state). Sand (0.075–4.75 mm) has low compressibility, good drainage, and high bearing capacity (depends on density and friction angle). Gravel has very high bearing capacity and excellent drainage. Silt is intermediate. Grain size directly governs behavior; fine soils are weaker and compressible; coarse soils are strong and stable.
Fine-grained soils (clay) have higher bearing capacity than coarse soils (sand), which is contrary to typical engineering principles
Drainage is independent of grain size; all soils drain equally fast, which is not supported by empirical evidence

rationale.a: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: Grain size is the primary classifier of soil behavior. Clay particles (< 0.005 mm) pack closely with no internal friction; cohesion (bonding between particles) provides strength. Clays are very compressible and drain slowly (low permeability). Sand particles (coarser) lock together via friction; cohesion is negligible. Sands are less compressible and drain quickly (high permeability). Gravel is strongest and drains best. Bearing capacity, compressibility, and drainage are all strongly correlated with grain size. This relationship is fundamental to geotechnical engineering and foundation design.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A site investigation reports soil with SPT N = 35 in sand at 18 m depth, overlain by clay with N = 8 at 5 m depth. The groundwater table is at 3 m depth. Recommend a foundation strategy and justify based on bearing capacity, settlement, and soil profile characteristics.

options.text: Use a shallow footing at 1 m depth on the surface; SPT data are not relevant to foundation selection, focusing on surface conditions

Use a shallow footing at 3 m depth (above groundwater) bearing on clay (N = 8). Bearing capacity is only 100–200 kN/m² (marginal); settlement will be moderate but acceptable, considering cost efficiency

Use a deep pile or caisson foundation extending to the sand at 18 m depth (N = 35). Sand provides high bearing capacity (400–800+ kN/m²) and low compressibility. Piles/caissons bypass the weak clay, achieving stable bearing and minimal settlement. Groundwater at 3 m requires special construction methods (casing, tremie if water entry occurs).
Use a floating foundation; groundwater at 3 m makes floating viable, reducing construction complexity

rationale.a: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: Clay at 5 m (N = 8) has marginal bearing capacity (100–200 kN/m²) and significant compressibility. This layer is unsuitable for anything but light single-story structures. The dense sand at 18 m (N = 35) has excellent bearing capacity (400–800+ kN/m²) and low compressibility. A deep pile or caisson foundation extending to the sand is the robust solution. Groundwater at 3 m is managed via casing during installation and tremie placement for bored piles. This strategy is typical for deep alluvial sites in the Philippines: bypass weak clay, anchor in strong sand.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: An SPT boring reaches a layer with N = 6 (blows per 300 mm). Classify the soil state and estimate the bearing capacity range.

options.text: SPT N = 6 is dense soil; bearing capacity > 800 kN/m².
SPT N = 6 is loose/soft soil; bearing capacity is approximately 100–200 kN/m² (marginal). Shallow footing design is risky; piles or deep foundations are preferred.
SPT N = 6 indicates perfect soil for any foundation; no further testing is needed.
SPT N = 6 is sand; clay cannot have N < 10.

rationale.a: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: SPT N = 6 falls in the 4 ≤ N < 10 range, indicating loose or soft soil with bearing capacity approximately 100–200 kN/m². This is marginal for shallow footings; differential settlement is likely. Deep foundations (piles or caissons) are preferred for structural loads.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: NSCP 2015 Section 101 (or appropriate foundation/soil section) (SPT Correlation with Bearing Capacity)
